did_you_know.text: The phrase “wise-hearted” refers not only to intelligence but also to practical skill and creative ability. The Torah presents the craftsmen’s talents as both a gift and a responsibility.
The phrase “whose heart moved him” describes someone who felt an inner desire to volunteer. The craftsmen came to the work not only because they were instructed, but because they wanted to help.
The phrase “morning after morning” emphasizes that the gifts arrived steadily, day after day. It shows enthusiasm that was not merely temporary.
The people brought so many materials that the craftsmen reported having more than the work required. Even great generosity needs careful management.
Moses ordered the donations to stop, and the people really did stop bringing them. This teaches that leadership also means knowing when to say, “Enough—we have what we need.”
The verse emphasizes that the materials were enough for all the work, with some left over. The project’s success was measured not only by beauty, but also by meeting the actual need.
The Tabernacle curtains combined rich colors with embroidered cherubim, making them both structural elements and works of art. Sacred work here involved planning, weaving, and design.
The curtain’s measurements are given in cubits, whose exact length is not known today. We can understand the proportions and general scale, but not determine the precise size in centimeters.
The gold clasps joined separate curtains into one system. In this way, many different parts became one Tabernacle.
Curtains made of goat hair were placed over the Tabernacle curtains as an additional tent layer. The structure therefore had several layers, not just one covering.
The inner curtains were joined with gold clasps, while the goat-hair curtains were joined with bronze clasps. The different materials fit the different roles of the Tabernacle’s layers.

Each board was about six and a half times taller than it was wide, so the walls were made of tall, narrow boards. If a cubit was roughly 45 centimeters, a board would have been about four and a half meters high, though this is only an estimate.

The curtain was decorated with cherubim, and later it is described as separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. It symbolized that even within a sacred space, there are boundaries and different degrees of closeness.
